notes:
1. e-Governance — Overview

  • e-Governance uses information and communication technology to improve government administration and public-service delivery.

Tamil Nadu’s e-Governance system combines:

  • Citizen-facing digital services.
  • Internal administrative reform.
  • Integrated data systems.
  • Grievance redressal.
  • Assisted last-mile access.
  • Emerging technologies.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Governance → Technology + Administrative Reform + Citizen Service Delivery

2. Meaning of e-Governance

e-Governance means the use of information and communication technology by government to improve:

  • Administration.
  • Delivery of public services.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Governance → Use of ICT in Government

3. Major Types of e-Governance Interaction

The four major interaction types are:

  • Government to Citizens → G2C.
  • Government to Business → G2B.
  • Government to Government → G2G.
  • Government to Employees → G2E.
📌 Must-Memorise

G2C → Citizens

G2B → Business

G2G → Government

G2E → Employees

4. Objectives of e-Governance

Effective e-Governance aims to improve:

  • Accessibility.
  • Speed.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Monitoring.
  • Citizen convenience.

5. Evolution of Digital Governance

The transition can be understood as:

Manual Administration → Digitisation → Integrated Digital Services → Data-Driven Governance

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

e-Governance is a progression beyond simple computerisation.

6. Computerisation and e-Governance

  • Converting paper forms into electronic forms alone does not constitute complete e-Governance.
  • True e-Governance also requires redesigning the way government functions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Computerisation ≠ Complete e-Governance

7. TNeGA Mission

  • Tamil Nadu e-Governance Agency seeks to improve citizens’ quality of life through efficient delivery of government services using information technology.
📌 Must-Memorise

TNeGA → Technology-Based Improvement of Government Service Delivery

8. Institutional Framework of e-Governance in Tamil Nadu

Tamil Nadu’s e-Governance initiatives are primarily coordinated through:

  • Directorate of e-Governance.
  • Tamil Nadu e-Governance Agency → TNeGA.

They function under the:

  • Information Technology and Digital Services Department.

9. Tamil Nadu e-Governance Agency — TNeGA

  • TNeGA functions as the state nodal agency for supporting and driving e-Governance initiatives of the Government of Tamil Nadu.

Its role includes:

  • Developing technology solutions.
  • Supporting government departments.
  • Integrating citizen services.
  • Promoting digital platforms.
  • Exploring emerging technologies.
📌 Must-Memorise

TNeGA → State Nodal Agency for e-Governance

10. Directorate of e-Governance

  • The Directorate of e-Governance provides the wider institutional mechanism for implementing and coordinating digital-government initiatives across departments.

11. Institutional Chain

The institutional relationship can be understood as:

State Government → Information Technology and Digital Services Department → Directorate of e-Governance / TNeGA → Departmental Digital Services

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

The purpose of coordination is to avoid completely isolated departmental digital systems without common standards or integration.

12. Tamil Nadu e-Sevai

  • Tamil Nadu e-Sevai is an important citizen-facing e-Governance platform.
  • It was developed by TNeGA.
  • It enables government services to be delivered electronically.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Sevai → Citizen-Service Delivery Platform

13. e-Sevai — Access Channels

Citizens can access e-Sevai services through:

  • Common Service Centres.
  • Direct citizen access through the online portal.

14. Objective of e-Sevai

e-Sevai seeks to:

  • Bring government services closer to citizens.
  • Enable end-to-end computerised applications.
  • Reduce manual intervention.

15. Important e-Sevai Services

Services available through the e-Sevai framework include:

  • Community Certificate.
  • Nativity Certificate.
  • Income Certificate.
  • First Graduate Certificate.
  • Widow Certificate.
  • Inter-Caste Marriage Certificate.
  • Legal Heir Certificate.
  • OBC Certificate.
  • Residence Certificate.
  • Small or Marginal Farmer Certificate.
  • Social-security pension applications.

16. e-Sevai Service-Delivery Chain

The transition can be understood as:

Government Office Visit → e-Sevai Centre / Portal → Electronic Application → Digital Processing → Service Delivery

17. Importance of e-Sevai

e-Sevai can reduce:

  • Repeated physical visits.
  • Travel.
  • Waiting time.
  • Paper handling.
  • Dependence on intermediaries.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Sevai → Citizen-Service Delivery Layer of Tamil Nadu e-Governance

18. e-District Programme

  • e-District is an electronic service-delivery programme operating at the district level.
  • Its objective is to provide citizen-centric government services electronically through e-Sevai Centres.

19. e-District Workflow

The e-District system connects:

Citizen → Service Centre → Department → Approving Authority → Electronic Service

20. Importance of e-District

District administration handles many high-volume services such as:

  • Revenue certificates.
  • Welfare applications.
  • Social-security services.

Digitisation reduces dependence on manual movement of paper files between offices.

21. e-District and e-Sevai — Difference

  • e-District refers broadly to the electronic processing architecture for district-level services.
  • e-Sevai is an important channel through which citizens access those services.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

e-District ≠ e-Sevai

e-District → Processing Architecture

e-Sevai → Citizen Access Channel

22. Common Service Centres — CSCs

Not every citizen has a:

  • Computer.
  • Smartphone.
  • Reliable internet connection.
  • Sufficient digital literacy.
  • Common Service Centres therefore function as assisted digital-service points.

23. Functions of Common Service Centres

CSCs can help citizens:

  • Access online services.
  • Submit applications.
  • Upload documents.
  • Obtain digitally processed services.

24. Importance of CSCs

  • An online portal may primarily serve digitally capable citizens.
  • A CSC provides human assistance to citizens who need support.
📌 Must-Memorise

Online Portal + Assisted Service Centre → Greater Digital Inclusion

25. Last-Mile Digital Inclusion

CSCs are particularly important for:

  • Rural residents.
  • Elderly persons.
  • Citizens unfamiliar with online systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Digital Service Without Requiring Digital Expertise from Every Citizen

26. Online Revenue Certificates

Revenue certificates are commonly required for:

  • Educational admissions.
  • Scholarships.
  • Welfare benefits.
  • Employment.
  • Legal purposes.

27. Revenue Services through e-Sevai

Electronic applications are supported for services including:

  • Community Certificate.
  • Income Certificate.
  • Nativity Certificate.
  • First Graduate Certificate.
  • Residence Certificate.
  • Legal Heir Certificate.

28. End-to-End Computerisation

The desired digital workflow is:

Application → Verification → Approval → Digitally Available Certificate

  • Electronic processing can reduce manual intervention.
  • Application status can be recorded within the system.
  • This improves administrative traceability.

29. Citizen Account

  • The e-Sevai portal provides citizen registration.
  • Citizens can sign in and apply for services directly.
📌 Must-Memorise

Office-Centred Government → Citizen-Centred Digital Government

30. Digital Land Records

Land administration is an important part of Tamil Nadu’s digital governance.

Official land e-services include access to:

  • Patta and FMB/Chitta information.
  • TSLR extracts.
  • A-Register extracts.
  • Patta verification.
  • Verification of poramboke land.

31. FMB

  • FMB stands for Field Measurement Book.
  • It contains survey-related land information.
📌 Must-Memorise

FMB → Field Measurement Book

32. TSLR

  • TSLR stands for Town Survey Land Register.
  • It is particularly associated with urban land records.
📌 Must-Memorise

TSLR → Town Survey Land Register → Urban Land Records

33. Importance of Digital Land Records

Digitisation of land records can improve:

  • Citizen access.
  • Verification.
  • Transparency.
  • Reduction in repeated visits to land-record offices.

34. Digital Land Records — Limitation

  • An online land record is only as reliable as the underlying administrative and survey data.
  • Accurate surveys, mutation and record updating remain essential.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digitisation of Land Records ≠ Automatic Elimination of Land Disputes

35. Mudhalvarin Mugavari

  • Tamil Nadu operates Mudhalvarin Mugavari as an integrated grievance-redressal mechanism.
  • e-Governance therefore extends beyond merely obtaining certificates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mudhalvarin Mugavari → Integrated Grievance Redressal

36. Mudhalvarin Mugavari — Grievance Channels

Citizens can submit grievances through channels including:

  • Web portal.
  • Mobile application.
  • Helpline.
  • Email.
  • Post and other supported channels.

The official system uses the helpline number:

1100

📌 Must-Memorise

Mudhalvarin Mugavari Helpline → 1100

37. Digital Grievance Tracking

  • A citizen receives a grievance ID after submitting a grievance through the portal.
  • The grievance ID can be used to track the case.

The sequence is:

Complaint → Acknowledgement → Tracking → Departmental Action

38. Grievance Redressal and Accountability

  • Digital grievance systems formally record complaints.
  • Their movement can be tracked.
  • This can improve administrative accountability.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

e-Governance = Service Delivery + Citizen Feedback + Grievance Redressal

39. e-Office

  • e-Governance must transform internal government functioning as well as citizen-facing services.
  • Tamil Nadu has been implementing e-Office across government institutions.
  • Its implementation has expanded to departments, Heads of Departments and subordinate offices.
📌 Must-Memorise

e-Office → Internal Administrative Digitisation

40. Functions of e-Office

A digital-office system can support:

  • Electronic files.
  • Digital movement of documents.
  • Online approval.
  • File tracking.
  • Reduced physical paper.
📌 Must-Memorise

Physical File → Electronic File

41. Administrative Benefits of e-Office

Electronic files can improve:

  • Speed.
  • Traceability.
  • Retrieval.
  • Monitoring.
  • Digital workflows can create a recorded sequence of actions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Citizen-Facing Digitisation + Internal Administrative Digitisation → More Complete e-Governance

42. SimpleGov

  • Tamil Nadu launched SimpleGov in November 2023.

It aims to:

  • Simplify government processes.
  • Digitise processes.
  • Re-engineer government processes.
📌 Must-Memorise

SimpleGov → November 2023

43. Government Process Re-engineering

Simply reproducing an old paper procedure on a computer does not necessarily improve administration.

The preferred sequence is:

Review Process → Remove Unnecessary Steps → Simplify → Digitise

44. Purpose of Process Re-engineering

Government Process Re-engineering seeks to:

  • Reduce unnecessary approvals.
  • Remove duplicate information.
  • Standardise procedures.
  • Increase automation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Complicated Manual Process → Complicated Online Process ≠ Administrative Reform

45. Importance of SimpleGov

  • SimpleGov represents movement from basic computerisation towards administrative redesign.
📌 Must-Memorise

SimpleGov → Process Reform, Not Mere Digitisation

46. Digital Welfare Platforms

Digital governance is increasingly used in welfare administration.

  • The planned Tamil Nadu State Schemes Portal was designed as a single-window platform.

Its proposed workflow covers:

Registration → Verification → Disposal → Sanction → Benefit Disbursal

47. State Scholarship Portal

  • Tamil Nadu has also developed a State Scholarship Portal framework.

It is intended to integrate:

  • Scholarship applications.
  • Direct Benefit Transfer across departments.

48. Direct Benefit Transfer — DBT

  • DBT stands for Direct Benefit Transfer.
  • It sends monetary benefits directly into beneficiary bank accounts.
📌 Must-Memorise

DBT → Direct Transfer of Monetary Benefits to Beneficiary Bank Accounts

49. Benefits of DBT

Potential administrative benefits include:

  • Reduced cash handling.
  • Better traceability.
  • Faster payments.
  • Easier reconciliation.

50. DBT — Important Distinction

  • DBT is a delivery mechanism.
  • It does not determine whether the welfare policy itself is appropriate.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

DBT ≠ Welfare Scheme

DBT → Method of Delivering Eligible Benefits

51. Single Sign-On — SSO

  • SSO stands for Single Sign-On.
  • TNeGA has developed and planned integration mechanisms using SSO.
  • SSO enables authenticated access across connected systems without requiring entirely separate authentication for every service.
📌 Must-Memorise

SSO → Single Sign-On

52. Interoperability

  • Interoperability means different government information systems can exchange and use information according to authorised standards.

The objective is:

Different Departments → Connected Digital Ecosystem

rather than:

Different Departments → Isolated Databases

53. Importance of Digital Integration

Integration can reduce:

  • Repeated data entry.
  • Duplicate documents.
  • Administrative delays.

However, greater integration increases the importance of:

  • Privacy.
  • Access control.
  • Cybersecurity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

More Connected Government → Greater Convenience + Greater Data Responsibility

54. Digital Governance in Education

  • Tamil Nadu increasingly uses digital platforms for educational administration and learning.
  • An important platform is EMIS.

55. EMIS

  • EMIS stands for Education Management Information System.
  • The Tamil Nadu School Education Department operates EMIS platforms for educational administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

EMIS → Education Management Information System

56. Functions of Education Digital Systems

Digital systems support:

  • School information.
  • Staff administration.
  • Examinations.
  • Educational programme management.
  • Digital public resources are also provided through the TN Schools ecosystem.

57. Education Data and Governance

Digital educational governance allows movement from:

School-Level Data → State-Level Information → Planning and Monitoring

58. Education Data Quality

  • Digital systems can improve monitoring only when the data entered is accurate.
  • Incorrect data does not become accurate merely because it is digitised.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digitally Available Information ≠ Automatically Reliable Information

59. Digital Governance in Health

  • Tamil Nadu is expanding digital administration in the health sector.
  • The state has moved towards HMIS 3.0.

60. HMIS

  • HMIS stands for Health Management Information System.

HMIS 3.0 is designed with improved:

  • Scalability.
  • Security.
  • Interoperability with other health-information systems.
📌 Must-Memorise

HMIS → Health Management Information System

61. HMIS 3.0 Implementation

  • In July 2025, Tamil Nadu issued orders for implementation of HMIS 3.0 across government medical facilities throughout the state.
  • C-DAC support was provided for implementation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

HMIS 3.0 → Government Medical Facilities → July 2025

62. Functions of Digital Health Systems

Digital health-management systems can improve:

  • Patient-information availability.
  • Hospital administration.
  • Monitoring.
  • Continuity of care.
  • Planning.

63. Privacy in Digital Health

  • Health information is highly sensitive.

Digital health governance therefore requires:

  • Authentication.
  • Access controls.
  • Data security.
📌 Must-Memorise

Better Health Data + Strong Privacy Protection

64. Tamil Nadu Geographical Information System — TNGIS

  • Tamil Nadu has developed the Tamil Nadu Geographical Information System through TNeGA.
  • GIS stores, analyses and visualises information connected with geographic locations.
📌 Must-Memorise

TNGIS → Tamil Nadu Geographical Information System

65. Purpose of TNGIS

TNGIS supports:

  • Spatial-data management.
  • Analysis.
  • Decision-making.

66. Government Applications of GIS

GIS can support planning in areas such as:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Land.
  • Water.
  • Public facilities.
  • Disaster management.

67. GIS and Spatial Decision-Making

Government can combine information such as:

Population + Roads + Hospitals

to identify areas with weak health-service access.

📌 Must-Memorise

Administrative Data + Location → Spatial Decision-Making

68. Importance of TNGIS

  • TNGIS shows that e-Governance is not limited to online transactions.
  • It can also support planning and decision-making.

69. Centre of Excellence in Emerging Technologies

  • TNeGA operates a Centre of Excellence in Emerging Technologies.

It explores technologies such as:

  • Artificial Intelligence.
  • Blockchain.
  • Data analytics.
  • Other emerging digital tools.

70. Artificial Intelligence in Governance

AI can potentially assist government with:

  • Pattern recognition.
  • Document processing.
  • Analytics.
  • Decision support.

71. Risks of Government AI

Government AI should avoid:

  • Unfair discrimination.
  • Non-transparent decisions.
  • Unaccountable automation.

72. Policy for Safe and Ethical AI — 2020

  • Tamil Nadu maintains a Policy for Safe and Ethical AI, 2020.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Safe and Ethical AI Policy → 2020

73. Blockchain Policy — 2020

  • Tamil Nadu adopted a Blockchain Policy in 2020.
  • It envisages blockchain applications for secure and transparent digital-service delivery.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Blockchain Policy → 2020

74. Blockchain — Government Use Case

  • TNeGA’s Centre of Excellence identifies tamper-resistant preservation of registration documents as one potential blockchain use case.

75. Emerging Technology — Key Principle

Technology should:

Solve a Governance Problem

rather than:

Be Adopted Merely Because It Is New

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

New Technology ≠ Automatically Better Governance

76. Cybersecurity in e-Governance

Government databases may contain information relating to:

  • Identity.
  • Land.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Welfare.

Unauthorised access can therefore create serious consequences.

77. Tamil Nadu Cyber Security Policy — 2020

  • Tamil Nadu maintains a Cyber Security Policy, 2020.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Cyber Security Policy → 2020

78. Three Important Tamil Nadu Digital Policies

Important 2020 policies covered in this chapter are:

  • Cyber Security Policy → 2020.
  • Policy for Safe and Ethical AI → 2020.
  • Blockchain Policy → 2020.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cybersecurity + Ethical AI + Blockchain → 2020

79. Cybersecurity Requirements

Strong digital government requires:

  • Authentication.
  • Access control.
  • Secure networks.
  • Data encryption.
  • Regular security monitoring.
  • Backup and recovery.

80. Privacy in e-Governance

  • Government should collect and use personal information only for lawful and legitimate administrative purposes.

81. Ethical AI Requirements

Automated systems should be:

  • Explainable where necessary.
  • Auditable.
  • Fair.
  • Accountable.
📌 Must-Memorise

Digital Convenience Must Not Come at the Cost of Citizen Rights

82. Trustworthy Digital Government

The relationship can be understood as:

e-Governance + Cybersecurity + Privacy → Trustworthy Digital Government

83. e-Governance and Good Governance

  • e-Governance is a tool for achieving good governance.
  • Technology can strengthen governance when it improves administrative processes and citizen services.

84. e-Governance and Transparency

  • Citizens can access information electronically.
  • They can track applications through digital systems.

85. e-Governance and Accountability

Digital systems can create records of:

  • Applications.
  • Decisions.
  • Movement of files.

This can improve administrative traceability.

86. e-Governance and Efficiency

  • Automation can reduce repetitive manual work.
  • Digital workflows can improve administrative speed.

87. e-Governance and Accessibility

  • Online portals allow citizens to access services without always travelling to government offices.

88. e-Governance and Responsiveness

  • Digital grievance platforms allow citizens to report problems.
  • They also allow grievances to be tracked.

89. e-Governance and Reduction of Discretion

  • Standardised workflows can reduce unnecessary discretionary interaction at routine administrative stages.

90. Digitisation and Good Governance — Distinction

  • Digitisation alone does not automatically produce good governance.
  • A poorly designed online system can merely digitise existing inefficiency.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digitisation ≠ Automatic Good Governance

📌 Must-Memorise

Good e-Governance = Technology + Process Reform + Accountability + Citizen-Centric Design

91. Digital Divide

Citizens differ in access to:

  • Smartphones.
  • Computers.
  • Internet connectivity.
  • Digital skills.
  • An online-only system may therefore disadvantage vulnerable groups.

92. Role of Assisted Digital Services

  • e-Sevai Centres and CSCs remain important even when direct online access expands.
  • They help reduce exclusion caused by differences in digital access and literacy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Direct Online Access + Assisted Access → Inclusive e-Governance

93. Language and Accessibility

Government digital platforms should be usable by:

  • Tamil-speaking citizens.
  • Persons with disabilities.
  • Citizens with limited digital literacy.

94. Fragmented Government Databases

Separate departmental databases can cause:

  • Duplicate records.
  • Inconsistent information.
  • Repeated verification.

95. Integration and Data Governance

  • Integration and interoperability can reduce fragmentation.
  • However, integrated systems require strong data governance.

96. Cybersecurity by Design

  • More digital services create a larger attack surface.
  • Security should therefore be incorporated from the design stage.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cybersecurity → Design Requirement, Not an Afterthought

97. Digital Exclusion

A citizen may be prevented from receiving an essential service because of:

  • Failed OTP.
  • Incorrect database entry.
  • Inaccessible portal.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digital Error Can Become Administrative Exclusion

98. Human Alternative

  • Essential services should retain practical mechanisms for citizens who cannot successfully use digital systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Digital Government Should Not Mean Digital-Only Government

99. Future Direction of Tamil Nadu e-Governance

Tamil Nadu’s e-Governance system is moving from:

  • Standalone Portals → Integrated Platforms.
  • Paper Files → e-Office.
  • Department Silos → Interoperability.
  • Manual Scheme Delivery → Digital and DBT-Based Delivery.
  • Administrative Data → GIS and Data Analytics.
  • Basic Automation → AI-Assisted Governance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Digital by Design, but Inclusive by Default

Important components include:

  • Directorate of e-Governance.
  • TNeGA.
  • e-Sevai.
  • e-District.
  • Common Service Centres.
  • Online revenue services.
  • Digital land records.
  • Mudhalvarin Mugavari.
  • e-Office.
  • SimpleGov.
  • Digital welfare platforms.
  • DBT.
  • SSO and interoperability.
  • EMIS.
  • HMIS 3.0.
  • TNGIS.
  • Artificial Intelligence.
  • Blockchain.
  • Cybersecurity.

101. Citizen-Facing e-Governance

Major citizen-facing systems include:

  • e-Sevai.
  • e-District-linked services.
  • Common Service Centres.
  • Online revenue certificates.
  • Land e-services.
  • Mudhalvarin Mugavari.

102. Internal Administrative e-Governance

Major administrative transformation mechanisms include:

  • e-Office.
  • SimpleGov.
  • Process re-engineering.
  • Integrated information systems.
  • Interoperability.

103. Data-Driven Governance

Major data-driven systems include:

  • EMIS.
  • HMIS 3.0.
  • TNGIS.
  • Data analytics.
  • Emerging AI-based tools.

107. TNPSC Traps

  • Computerisation is not complete e-Governance.
  • e-District and e-Sevai are not identical.
  • e-District is the broader district-level electronic processing architecture.
  • e-Sevai is an important citizen-access channel.
  • An online portal alone does not guarantee digital inclusion.
  • CSCs remain important for assisted access.
  • Digitising land records does not automatically eliminate land disputes.
  • Accurate survey and record updating remain necessary.
  • DBT is a benefit-delivery mechanism, not a welfare scheme itself.
  • Greater system integration also creates greater responsibility for privacy and cybersecurity.
  • Digitised incorrect data remains incorrect data.
  • AI-based administration must remain fair, accountable and appropriately explainable.
  • New technology should solve a governance problem rather than be adopted merely because it is new.
  • Digitisation does not automatically produce good governance.
  • An online-only service can contribute to digital exclusion.
  • A failed OTP or incorrect database record can become an administrative barrier.
  • Cybersecurity should be incorporated from the design stage.
  • Successful digital governance requires citizen-centric design and practical assisted alternatives.

  • Four major e-Governance interactions? → G2C, G2B, G2G and G2E.
  • G2C means? → Government to Citizens.
  • G2B means? → Government to Business.
  • G2G means? → Government to Government.
  • G2E means? → Government to Employees.
  • Is computerisation alone complete e-Governance? → No.
  • State nodal agency for e-Governance in Tamil Nadu? → TNeGA.
  • TNeGA functions under which department? → Information Technology and Digital Services Department.
  • Important citizen-facing platform? → Tamil Nadu e-Sevai.
  • Who developed e-Sevai? → TNeGA.
  • Two major e-Sevai access channels? → Common Service Centres and direct online citizen access.
  • e-District operates mainly at which level? → District level.
  • e-District and e-Sevai identical? → No.
  • Purpose of CSCs? → Assisted digital-service access.
  • FMB stands for? → Field Measurement Book.
  • TSLR stands for? → Town Survey Land Register.
  • TSLR is particularly associated with? → Urban land records.
  • Does land-record digitisation automatically eliminate disputes? → No.

  • Important cybersecurity requirements? → Authentication, access control, secure networks, encryption, monitoring, backup and recovery.

  • Good e-Governance requires? → Technology + Process Reform + Accountability + Citizen-Centric Design.
  • Why do CSCs remain relevant? → To support citizens affected by the digital divide.
